John F. Kennedy

Project 41 · presidential suite · from templates-president/kennedy.json · index · repo randomcase/john-f-kennedy

Democratic · 1961–1963 · the American standard: president 2 of the four who managed the war

Role. Managed early involvement: turned the adviser mission into a 16,000-man shadow army with helicopters and Special Forces, refused the combat troops his advisers asked for in 1961, and approved the coup that removed Diem.

Decisions, one line item each

1961-05Sends 400 Special Forces and 100 more advisers; approves covert operations against the North (NSAM 52).
1961-11After the Taylor–Rostow mission recommends 8,000 combat troops, sends advisers, helicopters and aircraft instead (NSAM 111). The one time combat troops were formally asked for and refused.
1962-02MACV created under Harkins; the adviser mission becomes a command.
1963-05Buddhist crisis begins at Hue; the regime's brutality becomes a nightly American story.
1963-08-24Cable 243: the administration signals it will not oppose a coup. Kennedy later calls the way it was sent a mistake, and does not withdraw it.
1963-10-11NSAM 263: plans to withdraw 1,000 advisers by the end of the year and most of the rest by 1965, 'without impairment of the war effort'.
1963-11-01Diem and Nhu overthrown and killed. Kennedy is shaken by the killings and not by the coup.
1963-11-22Assassinated. Whether he would have left in 1965 is the war's most argued counterfactual.

The Joint Chiefs, with their president

Chiefs in office during the term. A chief carried over from the previous president is listed once, with the earlier president, and given nothing more here — only the duty he owed this one, and, where it applies, his last days with him. The Joint Staff, the Pentagon, Arlington, Virginia. The Chairman’s office is on the E-ring, second floor, river side; the Chiefs meet in the “Tank”, Room 2E924, and from 1972 in the Gold Room next to it.

SeatWhoFromToWith this president
ChairmanGen. Lyman L. Lemnitzer19601962carried over from Dwight D. Eisenhower — Carried over from Eisenhower. Assured Kennedy the Bay of Pigs plan was sound; signed the Northwoods proposal in March 1962, which Kennedy rejected; sent to NATO that autumn. His duty to Kennedy lasted twenty-one months and ended in distrust on both sides.
ChairmanGen. Maxwell D. Taylor19621964The 1961 mission, then the chairmanship, then the embassy. Kennedy’s own choice, brought in over the Chiefs after the Bay of Pigs inquiry. Last days: Chairman on 22 November 1963. Had returned from Saigon with McNamara seven weeks earlier with the plan to withdraw 1,000 advisers; four days after Dallas signed on to NSAM 273, which kept the numbers and dropped the plan.
ArmyGen. George H. Decker19601962carried over from Dwight D. Eisenhower — Told Kennedy in 1961 that the Army could not win in Vietnam without going into the North; not reappointed.
ArmyGen. Earle G. Wheeler19621964 Kennedy’s Army Chief from October 1962. Last days: Army Chief on 22 November 1963; Chairman eight months later, and for the whole escalation.
NavyAdm. George W. Anderson Jr.19611963 Ran the quarantine in October 1962 and quarrelled with McNamara in Flag Plot over who commanded it; sent to Lisbon as ambassador.
NavyAdm. David L. McDonald19631967 CNO from August 1963. Last days: CNO on 22 November 1963, three months in.
Air ForceGen. Curtis E. LeMay19611965“Bomb them back into the Stone Age” was attributed to him; he said the ghostwriter put it in. Kennedy’s Air Force Chief. On 19 October 1962 told him the quarantine was “almost as bad as the appeasement at Munich”; Kennedy kept him and did not take the advice. Last days: Air Force Chief on 22 November 1963. Stayed through the start of Rolling Thunder.
Marine CorpsGen. David M. Shoup19601963carried over from Dwight D. Eisenhower — Carried over from Eisenhower; the one Chief who told Kennedy, with a map, how small Cuba was compared with the island he had taken at Tarawa, and how much it had cost. Last days: Commandant on 22 November 1963, five weeks from retirement.

Every nation that leaned on him

NationWhoWhenWhat
Soviet UnionKhrushchev1961–1963Vienna, June 1961: bullied over Berlin for two days and said afterward it was the worst thing in his life. Accepted the Wall in August rather than fight for East Berlin. Won October 1962, and gave up the Jupiters in secret to do it. Signed the test ban in 1963.
CubaCastro1961–1962Let the invasion go and refused the second air strike; paid $53 million in food and medicine for the prisoners; then the missiles. A separate nation with its own room, project 56.
LaosSouvanna Phouma, the Pathet Lao1961–1962The crisis Eisenhower warned him about. Chose a neutral coalition at Geneva (July 1962) over intervention; the Trail ran through the neutral country from then on. The test moved to Vietnam because he had declined it in Laos.
South VietnamNgo Dinh Diem1961–1963Diem took the money and the advisers and refused the reforms attached; Kennedy leaned back once, in the autumn of 1963, and Diem was dead within three months.
Francede GaulleMay 1961Told him in Paris that Vietnam was a bottomless military and political swamp. Not heeded; France was then leaned on in turn over NATO and the British entry to Europe.
United KingdomMacmillanDec 1962Nassau: when Skybolt was cancelled Macmillan asked for Polaris and got it, keeping Britain’s deterrent at America’s expense and provoking de Gaulle’s veto of British entry into the Common Market.
West GermanyAdenauer1961–1963Wanted a harder line on Berlin and got the Wall accepted instead; got the speech in June 1963.
Turkeyİnönü1962–1963The Jupiters were traded away over Ankara’s head and removed in April 1963 with a Polaris submarine offered in their place.
IndonesiaSukarno1962Pressed the Netherlands to hand over West New Guinea (August 1962) to keep Sukarno from Moscow; the Papuans were not asked.
IndiaNehruOct–Nov 1962When China attacked, Nehru asked for arms and aircraft and Kennedy airlifted them within days; non-alignment leaned, and was caught.
IsraelBen-Gurion1962–1963Sold the Hawk missiles, the first major US arms sale to Israel (August 1962), and asked for inspections at Dimona that he did not get.
EgyptNasser1961–1963Wheat under PL-480 to keep Nasser talking; recognised the Yemeni republic in December 1962 against Saudi and British objection.
PakistanAyub Khan1962Furious over the arms to India; leaned on Washington and was given assurances rather than arms.
CanadaDiefenbaker1962–1963Refused to put Canadian forces on alert during the missile crisis for two days and refused nuclear warheads for the Bomarcs; a State Department press release in January 1963 helped bring his government down.
